Section 1 defines MTD by three questions: what to move, how to move and when to move.
Section 1 describes the simulator's three modules: the network, the MTD mechanisms and the baseline attacker.
An MTD is designed by answering three questions: ``what to move'', ``how to move'' and ``when to move'' .

Figure 1 draws the simulator's three modules: the attacker, the network and MTD. MTD deploys its mechanisms at intervals, and each deployment reconfigures part of the network and disrupts the attacker.
The network in MTDSim is a three-layer hierarchical attack representation model (HARM) : a graph of hosts, in which each host runs services and each service carries vulnerabilities (Figure 1).
The host layer is the topology: the hosts are nodes, and an edge joins two hosts that can reach each other.
The exposed endpoints keep their address, software and accounts throughout: no MTD mechanism changes them, although a topology shuffle can change their links.
MTDSim deploys seven MTD mechanisms: five shuffles, two diversities, and no redundancy (Table 1).
Each reconfigures one part of the network: the host layer, the service layer or the users' credentials.
The deployment interval is the time between deployments: 200 s by default.
It is near-periodic: each interval is the set value plus a random delay of 0.5 s on average .

It follows a fixed procedure of six attack actions, modelled on the Cyber Kill Chain : it scans for hosts, enumerates one, scans its ports, exploits its vulnerabilities, brute-forces its accounts, and scans the neighbours of each host it compromises (Figure 1).
The attacker knows only its visible subgraph: the exposed endpoints, the hosts it has compromised and their neighbours.

It is persistent: in the definition of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), it pursues its objective repeatedly over an extended period and adapts to the defender's resistance .
It moves low and slow, trading speed for staying undetected : espionage intrusions go undetected for a median of 122 days, against 14 days across all intrusions .
And it is a threat defined by its objective: data exfiltration, impediment of mission-critical components, or positioning for future operations .
This dissertation groups the stages of published lifecycle models of an attack into four: preparation, intrusion, post-intrusion operations and actions on objectives.
The matrix lays out the top two levels: the 15 tactics as columns, each tactic's techniques beneath it (Figure 1).
It scales to many reports, but even identifying which techniques a report describes is not yet reliable: on the 50 most common techniques, the best systems reach 80 % precision at 66 % recall .
Cho et al. identify three: game theory, genetic algorithms and machine learning, with game theory dominating by volume .
Attackers are not necessarily rational: many aim only to exhaust a system's resources, and a strategy found against a rational attacker may not work against them .
Its attacker is the attacker model its training environment simulates : MTDShield's is the baseline attacker of Section 1 .
Cho et al. name four: analytical models, simulations, emulations and real testbeds .

The APT definition of Section 1 gives four: the APT attacker pursues its objective over an extended period (campaign persistence), uses different techniques after the foothold for different objectives (objective-specific behaviour), adapts to the defender's resistance (adaptivity) and moves low and slow to avoid detection (detection avoidance) .
The two surveys add the other four: choice of attack strategy, cost--benefit reasoning, learning and deployment-strategy awareness .
First, they lack adaptivity and learning: the attacker follows fixed attack patterns while the defender adapts and learns, although in practice the attacker is often the smarter of the two.
Second, they lack choice of attack strategy: few evaluations let the attacker choose among several attack strategies.
Third, they lack cost--benefit reasoning and deployment-strategy awareness: the attacker is seldom modelled as a rational actor, or as one that exploits how the MTD works.
awareness: an APT attacker learns the MTD's deployment patterns over time and looks for the logic of the deployment strategy .
They add detection avoidance: MTD is typically tested against active scanning, such as Nmap, while an APT attacker uses passive reconnaissance to stay hidden .

A \propstandin means a behaviour predicate is true, but not every predicate is true of its own behaviour: a predicate is false, or true only because its authors set the behaviour by a fixed rule, such as always re-scanning after a host-layer disruption, or assume it.
\paragraphBaseline attacker. The baseline attacker has campaign persistence: it repeats its six attack actions host by host until it reaches its goal, and carries on through every disruption .
It has choice of attack strategy in part: it can enter a host with stolen credentials, an exploit or brute force, but a fixed rule sets the order in which it tries them.
It has adaptivity in part: a fixed rule sets its response to each kind of disruption, such as always re-scanning after a host-layer disruption .
It has no cost--benefit reasoning: it orders the exploits on a host by return on attack (RoA), but that chooses which vulnerability to exploit, not which technique.

It has no objective-specific behaviour: after a foothold it takes the same six attack actions in either attack scenario, which changes only the host it attacks next and whether it gives up on it, and none of them exfiltrates or impedes.
It has no learning: an exploit of a vulnerability it has exploited before takes half the time , but it keeps vulnerabilities, not the patterns of MTD deployments, and the memory changes no choice.
It has no detection avoidance: it scans actively and does nothing to avoid an intrusion detection system (IDS).
It has no deployment-strategy awareness: nothing in it uses which mechanism deploys next or when it deploys.
It has campaign persistence in part: each attack path is a multi-stage chain of exploits, but each deployment interval's attack paths are computed afresh, so no campaign spans intervals.
It has no choice of attack strategy: it has every attack path to the database, but chooses none.
It has no adaptivity: its attack paths are recomputed after each MTD deployment, but no next technique is chosen from them.
It has no cost--benefit reasoning: it computes each attack path's cost and RoA, but no choice depends on them.
It has no objective-specific behaviour: every attack path leads to one objective, the database, and nothing follows once it reaches it.
It has no detection avoidance: the analytical model has no IDS for an attack path to avoid.
It has no learning: each deployment interval's attack paths are computed afresh, so nothing from earlier MTD deployments is kept.
It has no deployment-strategy awareness: nothing in the analytical model uses which mechanism deploys next or when it deploys.

Their attacker model is an automated attack script that runs four stages in a fixed order: it scans for web servers, collects the version of each web service it finds, exploits one known vulnerability of the Apache web server, and keeps a reverse shell, an outbound connection from the compromised server back to the attacker.
It has campaign persistence in part: each attack runs all four stages, but in one short attempt, and the next attack starts again with no knowledge of the network.
It has detection avoidance in part: the reverse shell is chosen ``in order to evade the detection by a defense system'' , but the testbed runs no IDS, so the evasion is assumed.
It has no objective-specific behaviour: after the foothold it keeps its shell and installs tools, but it has one objective, so no technique differs by objective, and none exfiltrates or impedes.

It has no deployment-strategy awareness: the attacker ``can determine the remaining available time'' before the next MTD deployment , when every mechanism deploys at once, so it predicts which mechanism deploys next and when, but no technique leverages the prediction.
It has no choice of attack strategy: every attack follows one attack scenario, in the same four stages.
It has no adaptivity: the script does not observe the MTD, and an attack that a deployment disrupts fails.
It has no cost--benefit reasoning: no technique's cost is weighed against its benefit.
It has no learning: the script observes no MTD deployment, and nothing is kept from one attack to the next.
\paragraphFinding. The three MTD attacker models still lack the properties of an APT attacker: only the baseline attacker has one in full, campaign persistence.
An MTD evaluation's result depends on its attacker model: the attacker model decides which deployment strategy is optimal (Section 1) and how effective MTD is (Section 1).
It is a proof of concept: it tests whether an attacker with more of an APT's properties changes what an MTD evaluation measures.
A step between two techniques of the same tactic is not an edge: the time an attacker spends within a tactic is its tactic duration (Section 1).
We built the attack graph from attack flows because they come from manual attack profiling: an analyst drew the order of every step.
The corpus is not limited to APT attackers: 18 of the 38 attack flows are attributed to a group in ATT | CK, criminal groups among them, and the other 20 name no group; one is an adware campaign.
Most edges between techniques come from one attack flow alone: 88 %, against 39 % of the edges between tactics (Appendix 1).
Tactics also make the tactic-to-action mapping smaller: it maps 15 tactics, rather than the 124 techniques the attack flows use, to MTDSim's six attack actions (Section 1).
The attack graph is sparsest before Initial Access: Reconnaissance appears in 10 of the 38 attack flows.
Data exfiltration and impediment each have an action in actions on objectives: the attacker steals data, or it impedes the victim's systems by encrypting, destroying or hijacking them.
We therefore asked two questions of each attack flow: did the attacker steal data, and did it impede the victim's systems?

The five attack flows of x did neither, so x is a mixed group, not a single objective: three attackers were removed from the network before they acted, one positioned for future operations, and one ran an adware campaign.

Before actions on objectives, the attack profiles share their most common tactics: Execution, Stealth, Discovery and Command and Control appear in more than half the attack flows of every attack profile.
Section 1 ablates the split: it runs the APT attacker model on the whole attack graph of Section 1 and compares the results with those of the four attack profiles.

No transition leads from a tactic back to itself: the time spent in a tactic is the delay of x. [Arcs x, x:] those of the chain x. [Weights x:] each timed transition has rate x, so that its delay has mean x, the mean duration of tactic x (Section 1).

[Initial marking x:] one token on Reconnaissance.
The single token means the attacker pursues one line of the campaign at a time: where an attack flow draws parallel branches, the token follows one of them.

It consists of three immediate transitions that none of their attack flows draws: from Reconnaissance to Resource Development, from Resource Development to Initial Access, and from Initial Access back to Reconnaissance, for an attacker whose intrusion fails.
A GSPN cannot route on the verdict: its weights are constants, or functions of the marking, and the verdict comes from MTDSim, outside the Petri net.
We therefore extend the GSPN with one element, the failure matrix x: a declared factor between zero and one for each pair of tactics (Section 1).

The APT attacker model integrates the two in one loop: the tactic the token reaches runs as one of MTDSim's attack actions, and the attack action's verdict selects the weights of the immediate transitions that take the token to the next tactic.
The attack flows cannot supply three inputs of the loop: the tactic-to-action mapping (Section 1), the tactic durations (Section 1) and the failure matrix (Section 1).
The vulnerability memory (Section 1) extends MTDSim's exploit attack action: each earlier success on a vulnerability raises the attacker's odds of exploiting it again.
These gaps set the ceiling of this dissertation: the APT attacker model can only be as good as the attack actions it adopts.

We also add one MTD effectiveness metric for a fourth property, adaptivity: time lost per MTD deployment, how much each deployment delays the attacker.

Section 1 sets out the experimental setup: the varied and held settings, runs, statistical analysis and ablation studies.
Section 1 compares the APT attacker model with and without each of three components: the attack profiles, the failure matrix and the vulnerability memory.
Each deployment strategy runs at six deployment intervals: 50, 100 and 200 s, which the earlier MTDSim studies ran, and 500, 1 000 and 2 000 s, up to ten times their longest (Table 1).

\paragraphStatistical analysis. Every interval is a 95 % confidence interval: Clopper--Pearson for ASP , the normal approximation for a mean, printed with x, and otherwise a percentile bootstrap over runs .
This section compares the APT attacker model with and without each of three components: the attack profiles, the failure matrix and the vulnerability memory.
At every deployment interval, the same three MTD mechanisms reduce NCR the most with the attack profiles and without them: IP shuffle, host topology shuffle and complete topology shuffle.
The failure matrix leaves time lost per MTD deployment unchanged: under IP shuffle and OS diversity at 2 000 s, the 95 % interval of the difference with and without it includes zero.

On objective-specific behaviour, the attack profiles' runs still differ in MTDSim, most of all in actions on objectives (Figure 1(a)): Exfiltration occurs only in x and x, Impact almost only in x and x, and neither in x. Each attack profile follows the order of tactics of its own attack flows (Section 1).
We attribute the APT attacker model's three properties and its lower ASP and NCR to the same two causes: its tactic durations and the order of its tactics.

In MTDSim, MTD disrupts the APT attacker model at these two points: its tactic durations set how likely a deployment is to cut an attack action short and fail it, and its failure matrix sets which tactic it takes after an attack action fails (Section 1).
Any difference between the two attackers comes from what the APT attacker model adds: the order of its tactics and four parts we declared (Section 1).
The APT attacker model is therefore comparable with the baseline attacker, and limited to what MTDSim's attack actions do: find and compromise hosts, with no actions on objectives.
This section says what that means for each of the three parts of an MTD evaluation that use the attacker model (Section 1): MTD modelling approaches, metrics and evaluation methods.

The APT attacker model shares the baseline attacker's six attack actions, so it is comparable with the baseline attacker and limited to what those attack actions do: find and compromise hosts, with no actions on objectives (Section 1).
